newsitem.title: USA: TWA Q1 beats forecasts but cash shrinks.
newsitem.headline: TWA Q1 beats forecasts but cash shrinks.

text.p: Trans World Airlines Inc cheered Wall Street with a smaller-than-expected first-quarter loss, but analysts cautioned that its lean cash balance gave the carrier little room for error.

TWA on Monday posted a first-quarter loss of $71.6 million, or $1.54 a share, on revenues of $762.3 million. The result beat analysts' expectations of a loss of $1.61 a share, according to First Call, though it exceeded the airline's 1996 first-quarter loss of $1.46 a share.

The St. Louis-based airline also said its cash position continued to decline. TWA had $136.5 million in cash and cash equivalents at the end of the March quarter, down from $181.6 million at the end of December. The company's cash balance has dropped more than half since the end of 1995.
"They need to build cash before next winter. The environment is strong, but I'm not sure they will be able to do that," said Glenn Engel, an analyst with Goldman Sachs.

Other analysts suggested that TWA's cash balance did not give it much of a cushion to survive cyclical industry downturns. By contrast, Continental Airlines Inc, the nation's fifth-largest airline, ended the March quarter with nearly $1 billion in cash on hand.
TWA had a difficult first quarter. Its auditors raised concerns about its ability to continue as "a going concern." The airline also was late in making some payments to some airports.

Those problems followed a series of setbacks last year related to the crash of Flight 800, the departure of former Chief Executive Jeffrey Erickson and a call by union machinists for the resignation of active CEO Gerald Gitner, who later became chairman.
Despite all that, the nation's seventh-largest carrier faces no immediate risk of bankrutpcy, analysts said.
"Airlines tend to last longer than people say they should," Engel said.
